title: MA8-07023
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXXXXX, a citizen of India, is claiming refugee protection under sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (hereafter the Act), alleging that she has a well-founded fear of persecution by reason of her membership in a particular social group and her political opinion. She is also alleging that she would be personally subjected to a risk to her life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, as well as to a danger of torture.

In her Personal Information Form (PIF), which she signed on July 23, 2008, the claimant1 alleged that while visiting India for a few weeks in XXXX and XXXX 2007, she encountered the following problems with police officers, and that because of these problems, she has a well-founded fear of persecution, of a risk to her life and of being subjected to torture should she have to return to live in her country.

The claimant alleged that a few days after arriving in the country, she met her friend, XXXXXXXX, whose brother, XXXXXXXXXX, had ties to the All India Sikh Students Federation and had been arrested and tortured by police in the past.

The claimant alleged that a few days later, on XXXX, 2007, as she was returning from the city of XXXX, the bus she was riding in with her friend and her friend's brother was stopped by police, who then asked her friend's brother to get out, which he did. She also alleged that she asked the driver to wait; since she was angry with the situation, she wanted to find out why her friend's brother had to get off the bus. However, her friend convinced her not to argue with the police officers.

The claimant alleged that later, her friend's father went to various police stations to find out what had happened to his son, XXXXXXXXXX, but that the police denied having arrested him. She also alleged that since she was angry about the situation, she decided to go with her friend's father to a police station, where she recognized the officer who had forced her friend's brother to get off the bus.

The claimant alleged that at the police station, she and her friend's father were unable to get satisfactory answers. She also alleged that the next day (XXXX, 2007), the police went to her home, arrested her, and took her to the police station along with her friend and her friend's father, where they questioned and beat her. She was released that day, after her father paid a bribe of 100,000 rupees.

The claimant alleged that her friend was not released and was raped by the police. She also alleged that after her friend was released from the police station, she and her friend's father left the village without a word to anyone.

The claimant alleged that on XXXXX, 2007, the police went to her home, arrested her and took her to the police station, where they took her photograph, fingerprinted her and forced her to sign blank documents. She also alleged that they questioned her about her friends, stating that she knew where they were and was secretly helping them, which she denied.

The claimant alleged that because of her answers, the police insulted her and struck her, which frightened her since she remembered that her friend had been raped. She also alleged that she was released that day, after her father paid a bribe of 75,000 rupees, on the condition that she not leave the village without the permission of the police.
The claimant alleged that after all of these incidents, she was badly shaken, and her family advised her to leave India and not to return, or she might have similar problems with the police.

On XXXX, 2007, the claimant left India and returned to work in XXXX, where she alleged she received a telephone call from an unknown individual, which upset her. She also alleged that she told her story to the wife of the couple for whom she was working as a XXXX, and that they advised her to come to Canada with them to save her life.
The claimant entered Canada with a valid visa on XXXXX, 2008. She claimed refugee protection in Canada on May 30, 2008.

The claimant also alleged in her PIF that since she left India, the police have created problems for her family and that an unknown individual again called her employers' home in XXXX to find out where she was.
State protection is the determinative issue in this case, although the credibility of the claimant's allegations was also analyzed.2

I am certainly aware of the importance of assessing all of the evidence presented in a refugee protection claim, including the narrative, which constitutes the primary source for understanding a claimant's personal situation. In this regard, the case law indicates that the circumstances, situations and events within a narrative must not be overlooked, otherwise, a travesty to justice could be the consequence. Moreover, this narrative must be understood in context, that is, in light of the documentary evidence regarding the country where the claimant is afraid to return to live.3 That said, it is possible to disbelieve a claimant's statements, but this should be stated unequivocally.4 In other words, there is an obligation to provide clear reasons for finding that a portion of testimony or evidence is not credible,5 after assessing the claimant's credibility and taking into account all of the evidence and testimony, as well as the fact that the claimant made his or her various statements under oath.6

It is well known that the issue of credibility is one of fact and cannot be determined by following a set of rules.7 It is also well known that a credibility finding is highly individualistic and often depends on intangible elements such as demeanour and the manner of testifying.8 Thus, the case law indicates that when a claimant has difficulty giving adequate and direct answers, the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) may draw an adverse inference from her demeanor at the hearing9 and, in certain circumstances, a claimant's conduct may be sufficient to reject her refugee protection claim,10 or a finding of non-credibility with respect to an important aspect of a claim can amount to a finding that there is no credible evidence on which the claim can be based.11 Credibility assessments being quintessentially questions of fact, there is generally a relative advantage for the decision-maker or the committee who heard the viva voce evidence.12

Given the individualistic nature of a determination of credibility, the decision-maker must be particularly careful to be and appear to be neutral, which requires the decision-maker to walk a delicate line. While the decision-maker may use common sense and wisdom gained from personal experience in observing and judging the trustworthiness of a person testifying before it on the basis of his or her narrative and demeanour during the hearing, the decision-maker must also avoid judging a refugee protection claimant's credibility on the basis of generalizations or matters that were not in evidence.13 In a context where this is often a claimant's only opportunity to be heard in person, it goes without saying that members who are responsible for assessing the credibility of the claimants must, at all times, be above reproach and objective and demonstrate that they paid attention to their personal situation and were interested in hearing their testimony.14 In addition, the decision-maker must avoid all behaviour that could be interpreted as constituting an appearance of bias.15

Before making my findings of fact and assessing the credibility of the claimant's allegations, I also carefully read the IRB Chairperson's guideline entitled Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution,16 as well as some decisions of the Federal Court of Canada that deal directly with this issue.17 In light of this information, I am particularly aware that extreme caution is required when reviewing the actions of women who are victims of violence; that in assessing these actions, specific knowledge must be used in order to reach a fair and correct judgment; and that in order to acquire this specific knowledge, it is necessary to discard myths and stereotypes about abused women.18 I am also aware that when making findings about the credibility of a woman who alleges that she was a victim of violence, I must be sensitive, knowledgeable and understanding about the reality of women who find themselves in such a situation;19 I must use a standard of reasonableness that, in fact, incorporates the experiences of women who are victims of violence;20 I must attempt to understand the evidence as a whole and in context;21 and if I have any doubt about the credibility of certain allegations, I must base my reasons on the evidence and on logic, and I must clearly explain those reasons.22

After conducting the hearing concerning this refugee protection claim and after considering all of the testimony heard and all of the documents submitted into evidence, I conclude that given her demeanour during the hearing, the claimant is not credible. I will explain. When she testified during the hearing, the claimant was very nervous, even anxious. At the beginning of her testimony, she was completely mistaken about the dates of the events that she allegedly experienced when she visited India in XXXX and XXX 2007. Finally, she started over and managed to recite what, in my opinion, she must have learned by heart. When I intervened to ask her some questions, she seemed unsettled and generally tried just to resume the story that she had previously memorized rather than give a direct answer to my question.

That being said, I am aware that during the hearing, I did not confront the claimant about this situation-namely, that she seemed to be reciting a narrative that she had previously memorized and that her overall credibility could be undermined by this. The case law establishes that during the hearing, the decision-maker must ensure that it confronts refugee protection claimants on every inconsistency, real or apparent, in their account of persecution, without criticizing, blaming, making disparaging comments or showing unjustified aggression and impatience.23 My finding of non-credibility does not result from any contradiction in the claimant's testimony (even though at the beginning of her testimony, she referred to dates that did not match those that she had written in her answer to question 31 of the PIF), but rather from the fact that in my opinion, this testimony as a whole had been previously memorized. However, given that during the hearing, I did not confront the claimant about the fact that she seemed to be reciting a narrative that she had memorized and that her overall credibility could be undermined because of this, I will not limit my analysis just to the issue of the claimant's credibility.

When asked during the hearing to state what she would fear if she were to return to India to live, the claimant answered that she is afraid of all police officers. When asked whether an arrest warrant had been issued or charges laid against her, the claimant answered that the police come to her parents' home from time to time, that they harass her father and that they are still looking for her. She added that they accused her of being involved with extremists, acting now from outside the country. Her statements in this regard were corroborated by an affidavit signed by her village's sarpanch.24

When asked to state where her parents are living today, the claimant answered that they still live in the same village. She also added that her father has been beaten by the police two or three times since she left the country. When asked whether she had included this information in her PIF, the claimant answered no. Asked to explain this omission, the claimant answered that it was only her mother who had given her this information over the telephone. Asked to explain why, at the beginning of the hearing, she had stated that the information in her PIF was complete, true and correct, she answered that she had just thought of this information during the hearing. In my opinion, these explanations are not reasonable, since the information omitted is directly related to the claimant's current fear of returning to live in her country and is not a detail that can be forgotten so easily. Consequently, the claimant's credibility is undermined regarding whether her father has been beaten by police officers since she left her country.

Asked during the hearing to state whether, following the incidents that she experienced in her country in XXX 2007, she had informed her country's authorities and tried to obtain their protection, the claimant answered no. When asked why she had not informed the authorities and tried to obtain their protection, the claimant answered that her father had simply told her to leave her country.

When asked what would prevent her from informing the authorities in her country and seeking their protection if she were to return to her country to live, the claimant answered that she was afraid that what had happened to her friend-namely, being arrested, detained and raped by police officers-could also happen to her.

It should be noted that the applicable test for whether state protection might reasonably be forthcoming must be objective.25 India is a democratic country, and there is a presumption that the state is capable of protecting its citizens.26 Generally, it is believed that in Punjab, rebels have become stakeholders and the normal political process has bounced back; there are no particular problems with respect to opposition politicians or opposition party members.27 In short, it is believed that the government of the state of Punjab and the federal government of India are democratic, and that the excesses do not unduly disrupt the political process. Moreover, the vibrant media and legal system in India are active.28

The documentary evidence also indicates that with respect to human rights, there are serious problems in India, especially the fact that police officers and members of the security forces engage in extrajudicial killings, torture and rape.29 The documentary evidence also indicates that the judiciary is independent and that in practice, the government generally respects judicial independence. However, the legal system is overburdened, which leads to significant delays and sometimes injustices, and citizens have also reported that judicial corruption is widespread.30 Moreover, human rights advocates believe that India's legal system is inadequate with regard to reporting cases of torture and allege that there is no independent agency to receive torture complaints and that there is no effective procedure for victims to remedy their situation.31 Some also believe that the guidelines and decisions from the Supreme Court of India aimed at reducing custodial deaths have failed to improve the overall situation.32

However, an individual or a non-governmental organization (NGO) can file a public interest litigation petition in certain courts, including the Supreme Court, alleging a need to seek redress of public injustice or injury.33 Moreover, the National Human Rights Commission was created in 1993 and mandated to investigate and intervene in cases of human rights violations, including in judicial proceedings.34 Even police forces have systems of control, and the police have their own code of conduct that they are to respect.35 There are also non-governmental organizations that help people having problems obtaining state protection, and in Punjab, a human rights commission was set up in 1997 and mandated to investigate complaints of human rights violations in the area.36

To rebut the presumption of state protection, relevant, reliable and convincing evidence that said protection is inadequate or non-existent must be adduced, and the applicable standard of proof is the balance of probabilities.37 Where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authority in place, and makes serious efforts to protect its citizens, the mere fact that it is not always successful at doing so will not be enough to rebut the existence of state protection.38 That said, state protection need not be perfect, but it must be adequate.39 Citizens are obligated to seek the protection of their country, except in cases in which it would be objectively reasonable not to; in other words, except if this protection would not be forthcoming anyway.40 In this regard, it is not reasonable to require refugee protection claimants to put their lives or the lives of their families in danger or to suffer greater persecution (which may consist of repeated discriminatory acts amounting to persecution) simply to demonstrate that state protection is ineffective.41 However, the fact that police officers act illegally within a specific region of a country cannot lead to the conclusion that the state as a whole is itself an agent of persecution or that it does not provide protection to the victims of the actions of said police officers.42 Additionally, the fact that a crime could not be solved does not prove that the police are ineffective.43 Finally, the existence of deficiencies in fundamental rights must be considered when analyzing the presumption of state protection for citizens in India or any other country.44

During her submissions, the claimant's lawyer stated that in this case, the state was the agent of persecution since the claimant was persecuted by police officers, and she suggested that consequently, the claimant was not obligated to seek protection from her country's authorities. With the greatest respect for the opposite view, I am of the opinion that this suggestion does not match the state of the current case law, although a few decisions have apparently, at some point, supported this statement.45 In my opinion, the real question to be asked is whether it is reasonable to require the claimant to seek protection from her state, in any way, even in cases in which the police are the persecuting agent.46

During her submissions, the claimant's lawyer also stated that there are very serious problems with the police in India, including the fact that some of them torture detainees, which is corroborated by the documentary evidence.47 She stated that in that context, the claimant could never be protected if she were to testify against the police. In short, in her view, seeking state protection in India against police officers who acted illegally can make matters much more dangerous and, therefore, state protection in India is inadequate.

The situation in India is obviously problematic, with serious human rights violations being committed, including by police officers.48 Does noting that such human rights violations are still today alarmingly widespread in India and that certain politicians, police officers and members of the security forces commit these violations amount to a conclusion that state protection in India is inadequate? It does not, in my opinion, because certain police bodies and judges have intervened and convicted police officers who committed serious human rights violations.49 The Indian constitution and decisions from the Supreme Court of India limit the powers of the police with respect to arresting and detaining50 a person and condemn torture.51 Furthermore, aside from her subjective analysis of the situation, the claimant submitted no documents that might have established, on one hand, that in India, all police officers work in a coordinated manner, without questioning the legality of their colleagues' actions, or, on the other hand, that simply because she approached a judicial authority-for example, to report what she was put through by certain police officers-this would have immediately placed her in a situation in which she would have been subjected to a risk to her life, a danger of torture or a risk of even greater persecution. The claimant and her lawyer also did not draw my attention to the most relevant passages specifically included in the documentary evidence52-passages that might have supported the claimant's subjective analysis regarding these two precise questions. In the absence of exceptional circumstances established by the claimant, I am of the opinion that it must be taken for granted that there is a fair and independent judicial process in India.53 That being said, I did not limit myself to that fact, and I conducted what I deem to be a thorough analysis of the documents submitted into evidence in this file.

In her country, the claimant has the support of a lawyer, who took steps for her, and of a sarpanch, who signed an affidavit corroborating her allegations about the illegal acts committed against her or against her family by police officers.54

Given the fact that the claimant's credibility was undermined for the reasons set out in the preceding paragraphs; given all of the documentary evidence, in which both the positive and negative aspects of the situation are analyzed;55 and given the personal situation of the claimant, who obtained a letter from a lawyer and an affidavit from her village's sarpanch that both corroborate her main allegations, I find that the claimant's testimony and the arguments made by her lawyer during her submissions do not constitute convincing evidence that, in her personal case, rebuts the presumption that the Indian authorities are capable of protecting its citizens.

Furthermore, I am of the opinion that in this situation, it was not unreasonable to expect the claimant to have informed her country's authorities in the past or to inform them in the future, if necessary, with assistance from governmental or non-governmental organizations specializing in human rights, in order to alert the Indian authorities, particularly by seeking legal redress, and to seek their protection by indicating the fact that she had been illegally arrested, detained and beaten by police officers, or even by indicating that she fears retaliation in the future from these very police officers.56 Her explanations-that she did not initiate any steps and that in the future, she would be afraid to seek remedies against the police officers because according to her, she would be at risk of retaliation from these very police officers, and that state protection is inadequate-are unsatisfactory given that according to the documentary evidence, democracy still operates in India despite the persistence of serious problems, and on the whole, India has resources, particularly via its judicial apparatus, but also via specialized human rights organizations that can help people seeking state protection,57 and is willing to provide adequate protection to its citizens.58 In short, I am of the opinion that the claimant did not file any evidence establishing that she did what was necessary, in the circumstances and in the context, to alert the Indian authorities and to try to seek their protection, or even that it would be impossible to do so in the future.59 CONCLUSION
Consequently, I determine that the claimant is not a Convention refugee under section 96, or a person in need of protection under subsection 97(1) of the Act.

For these reasons, her refugee protection claim is rejected.
